fixes.explanation: Olive oil, yes! Ephraim "…makes a covenant with Assyria and sends olive oil to Egypt." Assyria gets the covenant, and Egypt gets the olive oil. Ephraim has his hands in both places.

False is right. The text says, "He will punish Jacob according to his ways and repay him according to his deeds." The word is according, so it's tied to ways and deeds. The punishment follows what has been done.
Heel is it! "In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel…" The man was holding on before he'd even been introduced to anybody. I've got a mustache for hands, and I still wouldn't try that.

Arm is a fair guess, friend, since a grab like that sounds like an arm job. But the text is more specific: "In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel…" Down at the bottom, the heel. Nobody's guessing arm after that one.
That's it, baker. The text says "he wept and sought His favor…" So the story doesn't stop at the win. The wrestler is crying and asking for favor, and the text also says he found Him at Bethel.
No silent walk-off here, friend. The text says Jacob "…wept and sought His favor…" and that "he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there…" Walking off isn't what the text shows.

You'd expect a victory lap, friend, and I'd probably take two. But the text says Jacob "…wept and sought His favor…" Tears, not a boast. He struggled with the angel and prevailed, and he also wept and sought His favor.

Yes! "But you must return to your God…" After Jacob's story comes that "But," and the prophecy turns. It's a call to come back to God, plain and direct. And I think it lands softer than it sounds, since Jacob wept and sought favor and found Him.

Giving it all away isn't what Ephraim says, friend. He says, "How rich I have become! I have found wealth for myself." Then he claims, "In all my labors, they can find in me no iniquity that is sinful." His claim is about having no sinful iniquity.

Tents! The LORD says, "I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast." Notice the word again. It says dwelling in tents has happened before, and the LORD ties it to the days of the appointed feast.

Cities are a fair guess, friend, since that's where most folks settle down. But the text says, "I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast." The answer is tents. Nobody's calling a realtor for this one.

Yes, that's the one. The text says, "…their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field." The question is about sacrificing bulls in Gilgal, a town in Israel, and it's the altars that become those heaps. Those altars won't stay standing.

Lasting forever would be a big promise, and the text doesn't make it. It says, "…their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows of the field." Heaps of stones in a field, friend. That's the opposite of a pillar, and nobody's putting a plaque on a pile.

A wife, yes! The text says, "…Israel worked for a wife—for a wife he tended sheep." Same man as Jacob, since Genesis 32:28 says his name was changed to Israel. Sheep for a wife, friend. That's quite a story.
Folks work for houses every day, friend, so I'd believe it. But the text says, "…Israel worked for a wife—for a wife he tended sheep." The answer is wife, and the sheep were for her.

A prophet, yes! "But by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved." The LORD is the one doing the bringing out, and He does it by a prophet. The same line says that by a prophet Israel was preserved.

That's right, and I think this one is heavy. The text says, "…his Lord will leave his bloodguilt upon him…" The line comes after Ephraim has provoked bitter anger. It goes on to say his Lord will repay him for his contempt.
